skill.name: chipsec
skill.description: Analyze offline UEFI and BIOS firmware dumps with Intel CHIPSEC. Use it to decode firmware structure, inventory EFI executables, check known threats, extract NVRAM variables, and parse SPI descriptors.
skill.summary: Analyze offline UEFI and BIOS firmware dumps with Intel CHIPSEC.
skill.author: BrownFineSecurity

security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives caused by Markdown command examples, defensive malware terminology, and firmware file extensions. The confirmed risks are repeated setup instructions that use sudo and chmod 777 under Python site-packages, which create unsafe global write permissions.

remediation.issue: Unsafe global CHIPSEC log directory workaround
remediation.suggestion: Remove sudo chmod 777 guidance and document a user-writable virtual environment, local log directory, or least-privilege permission fix.

remediation.issue: Command examples rely heavily on shell execution
remediation.suggestion: State that commands require user approval, quote user-supplied paths, and avoid unnecessary command substitution in examples.

remediation.issue: Offensive security wording may confuse reviewers
remediation.suggestion: Replace post-exploitation phrasing with authorized incident response language and keep the offline-only scope prominent.

content.value_statement: Firmware dumps are difficult to review without repeatable tooling. This skill guides offline CHIPSEC workflows for threat checks, inventories, structure decoding, and reporting.
actual_capabilities: Runs offline CHIPSEC workflows against UEFI, BIOS, ROM, FD, CAP, and FV firmware files.
Guides known threat checks with the CHIPSEC UEFI blocklist module.
Generates EFI executable inventories with hashes for baseline comparison.
Decodes firmware structure and identifies extracted firmware volumes, files, sections, and NVRAM output.
Explains SPI flash descriptor parsing with platform hints.
Helps interpret CHIPSEC results, exit codes, and threat match details.
limitations: It requires CHIPSEC and supporting command-line tools to be installed separately.
It is intended for offline firmware dumps, not live system security checks.
Known threat detection depends on CHIPSEC blocklists and firmware format support.
It does not prove a device is clean when no known signature is found.

use_cases.title: Review a Firmware Dump
use_cases.description: Run an offline CHIPSEC workflow to scan, decode, inventory, and document one firmware image.

use_cases.title: Compare Firmware Updates
use_cases.description: Create inventories before and after an update, then identify changed EFI modules and hashes.

use_cases.title: Support Incident Response
use_cases.description: Check a suspect firmware image against known CHIPSEC signatures and a trusted baseline.

prompt_templates.title: Start a Basic Firmware Scan
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner workflow for a single firmware file.
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze this firmware dump with the chipsec skill. Explain each step before running commands and save the results in an organized folder.

prompt_templates.title: Create an EFI Inventory
prompt_templates.scenario: Build a baseline for later comparison.
prompt_templates.prompt: Generate an EFI executable inventory for this firmware image. Summarize module names, hashes, and any entries that need follow-up.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Two Firmware Images
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare these two firmware dumps with CHIPSEC inventory checks. Highlight changed, added, or removed EFI modules and explain the security impact.

prompt_templates.title: Investigate a Suspect Firmware Dump
prompt_templates.prompt: Perform an offline CHIPSEC incident response review. Run known threat checks, decode structure, inspect NVRAM output, and produce a prioritized findings report.

output_examples.input: A user provides a laptop BIOS ROM and asks for a first-pass review.
output_examples.output: The skill runs a threat scan, creates an EFI inventory, decodes the firmware, and summarizes whether CHIPSEC reported known matches.

output_examples.input: A user provides old and new firmware images after a vendor update.
output_examples.output: The skill compares inventories, lists changed modules, flags unexpected differences, and recommends manual review for high-impact components.

output_examples.input: A user provides a suspect IoT firmware dump from an authorized investigation.
output_examples.output: The skill checks known signatures, extracts available structure, records relevant hashes, and prepares a concise incident response summary.

best_practices: Analyze only firmware that you own or have explicit authorization to review.
Keep original firmware files unchanged and write analysis output to a separate directory.
Treat CHIPSEC matches as leads that need validation with hashes, GUIDs, and vendor context.
anti_patterns: Do not run live system CHIPSEC modules through this offline workflow.
Do not make system-wide permission changes unless you understand the security impact.
Do not assume that a clean blocklist scan means the firmware is safe.

faq.question: Does this skill require root access?
faq.answer: The intended workflows use offline firmware files and no kernel driver access. Some setup guidance in the source still needs safer wording.

faq.question: Which firmware formats are covered?
faq.answer: The skill discusses BIN, ROM, FD, CAP, SCAP, FV, and full flash dump files.

faq.question: Can it detect all firmware malware?
faq.answer: No. It can check known CHIPSEC signatures, but unknown implants require deeper reverse engineering and external validation.

faq.question: Can it compare firmware versions?
faq.answer: Yes. It guides inventory generation and comparison so changed EFI modules can be reviewed.

faq.question: Does it replace UEFITool or binwalk?
faq.answer: No. It can complement those tools by adding CHIPSEC-specific scans, inventories, and result interpretation.

faq.question: Is this suitable for production device attestation?
faq.answer: No. It supports analysis of firmware dumps, but production attestation requires a controlled process and trusted measurements.
